Gynecol Obstet Fertil 2006; 34: 147–53. Administration in renal impairment. Although unexpect- ed, renal impairment reduced raloxifene clearance in a pharma- cokinetic study (see above). Licensed product information in the UK contra-indicates the use of raloxifene in severe renal impair- ment, and in the USA it advises caution in moderate and severe impairment. Nevertheless, raloxifene has been studied in post- menopausal women with renal impairment and severe osteope- nia or osteoporosis. An oral dose of 60 mg daily for 1 year was given to 25 women on haemodialysis and found to improve bone mineral density of the lumbar spine, compared with 25 women given placebo; there were no reported adverse effects.1 1. Hernández E, et al. Effects of raloxifene on bone metabolism and serum lipids in postmenopausal women on chronic hemodialy- sis. Kidney Int 2003; 63: 2269–74. Hyperparathyroidism. The effects of raloxifene have been reported in postmenopausal women with mild primary hyperpar- athyroidism (p.1087). Reductions in markers of bone turnover and plasma concentrations of calcium have been described in an observational report1 and a small, short-term, placebo-controlled study.2 An increase in bone mineral density was also detected after 12 months of treatment with raloxifene.1 1. Zanchetta JR, Bogado CE. Raloxifene reverses bone loss in post- menopausal women with mild asymptomatic primary hyperpar- athyroidism. J Bone Miner Res 2001; 16: 189–90. 2. Rubin MR, et al. Raloxifene lowers serum calcium and markers of bone turnover in postmenopausal women with primary hyper- parathyroidism. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2003; 88: 1174–8. Malignant neoplasms of the breast.
